Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette: Ana Gómez had always taken pride in her work as a detective. For over two decades, she had been driven by a strong sense of justice and a determination to protect others. But all that changed on the day she was exposed to toxic chemicals while investigating a warehouse fire. The memories of that event still felt like they were happening right now - not just fragments, but the sensations, too: the feeling of her airway constricting as she struggled to breathe, the smell of sweat and antiseptic that clung to her skin. In the months following the incident, Ana began to notice subtle changes in herself. She was more jumpy than usual, always on edge when unexpected sounds caught her off guard - a car backfiring, a door slamming shut. Her colleagues started to comment on how tense she seemed all the time, like her body was coiled and ready to spring into action at any moment. Ana couldn't shake the feeling that danger lurked around every corner, waiting to pounce. As a detective, Ana had always relied on her sharp instincts to scan for potential threats. But now, this hyper-vigilance seemed more like a curse than a blessing. She found herself constantly scanning her surroundings, even when she was off-duty - in the grocery store, at home with her family. Her ex-husband had complained about it during their divorce proceedings, saying that Ana's constant "on-edge" behavior had made him feel like he was walking on eggshells around her. Ana tried to push these feelings away by redirecting her thoughts whenever they arose. She'd focus on something else - a case she was working on, a TV show she liked - but the tension remained, simmering just below the surface. And then there were the triggers: certain smells could send her spiraling back into that warehouse, gasping for air. Sweat or body odor would transport her to the hospital where she'd spent weeks recovering from her exposure, feeling helpless and scared. The worst part was when Ana caught sight of authority figures - police officers, firefighters, even medical personnel in their crisp uniforms. She knew it didn't make sense; these were people who were supposed to help others, just like she did. But something about their confidence and composure triggered a deep-seated anxiety within her. It made her feel lost, like she was floating outside of herself, unable to reconnect with the world around her. Ana had always prided herself on being stoic, unflappable in the face of danger. But now, even small setbacks sent her reeling. She felt like a part of her had been irreparably damaged during that warehouse fire - not just her lungs, but something deeper and more fundamental to who she was as a person. One day, while investigating a routine case, Ana found herself standing outside the hospital where she'd spent so many weeks recovering from her exposure. Something about the sight and smell of it sent her tumbling backward in time, her memories colliding with each other like jagged pieces of glass. She stumbled away from the scene, feeling raw and exposed. For a while after that incident, Ana tried to hide behind her mask of professionalism, but the truth was starting to seep out: she couldn't do this anymore. The constant hypervigilance, the triggers that sent her careening back into the past - it was all taking its toll on her relationships and her work. That's when Ana finally realized she needed help. She scheduled an appointment with a therapist, terrified of facing what lay ahead but knowing she couldn't keep running from herself forever. What frightened Ana most was that she'd lost touch with her emotions, like they were locked away behind some impenetrable wall. She longed to feel whole again - not just as a detective, but as a person.
